assignment.title: Factoring Polynomials — Honors
assignment.essentialQuestion: How does the structure of the expression influence the selection of an efficient method for factoring polynomial expressions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Honors version of Bluebonnet Algebra II — Polynomials, Lesson 1 (Factoring Polynomials), TEKS A2.7E (A2.7D). One assignment for the whole lesson. Beyond the regular lesson: quadratic form and substitution (x⁴, x⁶, and (x + 1)³ − 8), grouping that needs rearranging or six terms, a⁶ − 64 two ways and reconciled, sums that still factor (x⁴ + 64), error analysis with a numeric check, parameter questions, a box model, and a divisibility proof. Factoring answers are graded by their factors (any order; a minus sign may move between factors) and must be completely factored; intermediate boxes ask for the exact intermediate step. Practice includes two audited SAT items (MathMaster CCMR bank). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Getting started — factor ${{a}}x^2 {{b|xterm}} {{c|signed}}$ with the $ac$ method.
hints: Multiply a and c. Then look for two numbers with that product whose sum is the x-coefficient.
Split the middle term with those two numbers and factor by grouping.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In the ac method for ax² + bx + c, the two numbers you look for add to…

solutionReview.headline: Find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term, and group.
reasoning: {{m1}} and {{m2}} have product {{ac}} and sum {{b}}, so {{a}}x² {{b|xterm}} {{c|signed}} = {{a}}x² {{m1|xterm}} {{m2|xterm}} {{c|signed}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Two numbers with product c (not ac) only work when a = 1.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: ${{g}}x^4 - {{gk4}}$
hints: Take out the GCF first.
x⁴ is the square of x², so the next step is a difference of squares — and one of the factors it leaves is again a difference of squares.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For any number k, x⁴ − k⁴ first factors as…

solutionReview.headline: GCF, then the difference of squares twice.
reasoning: x² − {{k2}} = (x + {{k}})(x − {{k}}), and x² + {{k2}} is a sum of squares, which is prime.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at {{g}}(x² + {{k2}})(x² − {{k2}}): x² − {{k2}} is still a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Find the positive value of $b$ that makes $x^2 + bx + {{c2}}$ a perfect square trinomial, then factor the trinomial.
hints: In (x + c)², the middle term is 2 · x · c.
The constant term {{c2}} is the square of which positive number?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x + c)² expands to…

solutionReview.headline: A perfect square trinomial is (x + c)² = x² + 2cx + c².
solutionReview.commonError: Taking b = {{c}}: the middle term of (x + c)² is 2cx, not cx.

questions.prompt: Factor $2xy + 3z + 6y + xz$ by grouping. The first two terms share no factor, so rearrange the terms before you group.

responses.label: A different grouping also works. Which one?

steps.title: Grouping needs the right pairs
steps.instruction: Factoring by grouping works only when each pair shares a factor AND the binomials left inside match. If the written order fails, rearrange.

hints: Look for two terms that share a variable: 2xy and 6y both contain y.
After grouping, factor the GCF out of each pair; the binomials left inside must match.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What factor do 2xy and 6y share?

solutionReview.headline: Rearrange so each pair shares a factor.
reasoning: Both groups contain (x + 3), so 2y(x + 3) + z(x + 3) = (x + 3)(2y + z).
Grouping 2xy with xz works too: x(2y + z) + 3(2y + z) = (x + 3)(2y + z).
solutionReview.commonError: Grouping 2xy with 3z: they share no factor, so the method seems to fail — it is the grouping that failed, not the polynomial.

questions.prompt: Factor $ax^2 + bx^2 - 5ax - 5bx + 6a + 6b$ completely. Group the six terms in three pairs, factor each pair, factor out the common binomial — and keep going.

steps.title: More than four terms
steps.instruction: Look for groups that all leave the same binomial. Example: px² + qx² + 2px + 2qx + p + q = x²(p + q) + 2x(p + q) + 1(p + q) = (p + q)(x² + 2x + 1) = (p + q)(x + 1)².

steps.title: Factor completely
steps.instruction: After the common binomial comes out, check every factor again.

hints: Pair the two terms with x², the two terms with x, and the two constants.
Each pair contains the same binomial.
Is the trinomial that is left factorable?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ax² + bx² factors as…

solutionReview.headline: Three pairs, one common binomial, then the trinomial.
reasoning: ax² + bx² = x²(a + b), −5ax − 5bx = −5x(a + b), 6a + 6b = 6(a + b).
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at (a + b)(x² − 5x + 6): the trinomial still factors.

questions.prompt: Quadratic form. Find the linear factors of $f(x) = x^4 - 13x^2 + 36$: substitute $u = x^2$, factor the quadratic in $u$, substitute back, and check every factor again. Then list the zeros of $f$ and check them against the table of values.

responses.label: Zeros of f, as a set

steps.title: Quadratic form
steps.instruction: A polynomial is in quadratic form when it can be written au² + bu + c, where u is an expression in x. In x⁴ − 13x² + 36, x⁴ = (x²)², so u = x².

steps.title: Keep going
steps.instruction: After substituting back, a factor may still be a difference of squares or cubes.

steps.title: Zeros from factors
steps.instruction: If x − r is a factor of P(x), then P(r) = 0: at x = r that factor is 0, so the whole product is 0. Each linear factor gives a zero, and each real zero c is an x-intercept (c, 0) of the graph.

hints: Two numbers with product 36 and sum −13.
Replace u with x² in each factor.
After substituting back, check each factor: is it a difference of squares?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Why is u = x² the right substitution for x⁴ − 13x² + 36?

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, factor, substitute back, factor again.
reasoning: Each factor is a difference of squares: (x − 2)(x + 2)(x − 3)(x + 3).
Each linear factor is 0 at one value, so the zeros are −3, −2, 2 and 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at (x² − 4)(x² − 9): both factors are still differences of squares.
solutionReview.connection: The zeros ±2 and ±3 are where y = x⁴ − 13x² + 36 crosses the x-axis.

questions.prompt: Factor $2x^4 - 7x^2 - 4$ completely. With $u = x^2$ the leading coefficient is 2, so factor $2u^2 - 7u - 4$ with the $ac$ method.
hints: Find two numbers whose product is a · c and whose sum is −7.
Substitute back u = x². Which factor is a difference of squares?
A positive multiple of x² plus a positive number has no real zeros, so it is prime.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. After substituting back, the factor 2u + 1 becomes…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, use the ac method, substitute back.
reasoning: a · c = 2 · (−4) = −8; the numbers 1 and −8 have product −8 and sum −7.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing (2x + 1)(x − 4): u stands for x², so every u becomes x².

questions.prompt: Factor $x^6 - 7x^3 - 8$ completely. Use $u = x^3$; after you substitute back, each factor is a sum or difference of cubes.
hints: Two numbers with product −8 and sum −7.
After substituting back, write each constant as a cube.
a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) and a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which number cubed is 8?

solutionReview.headline: Quadratic form first, then the two cube patterns.
reasoning: x³ − 8 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4) and x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² − x + 1); both trinomials are prime.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² + x + 1): for a SUM of cubes the middle sign is negative.

questions.prompt: Substitution works for any repeated expression. Factor $(x + 1)^3 - 8$ completely: let $u = x + 1$, factor $u^3 - 8$, substitute back, and simplify each factor.
hints: u³ − 8 is a difference of cubes: 8 = 2³.
Replace u with (x + 1), expand (x + 1)², and combine like terms.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If u = x + 1, then u − 2 equals…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, factor the difference of cubes, substitute back, simplify.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving the factor as (x + 1)² + 2(x + 1) + 4: it is right but not simplified.

questions.prompt: One polynomial, two first steps. $a^6 - 64$ is a difference of squares, $(a^3)^2 - 8^2$, and a difference of cubes, $(a^2)^3 - 4^3$. Factor it completely starting with squares. Then explain why starting with cubes seems to give a different answer.

responses.label: Cubes first gives (a² − 4)(a⁴ + 4a² + 16) = (a − 2)(a + 2)(a⁴ + 4a² + 16). Which statement is true?
options: a⁴ + 4a² + 16 is not prime: it is the product of the two quadratic factors from the squares-first method, so both methods agree
a⁴ + 4a² + 16 is prime, so the two methods give different complete factorizations
Cubes first is not allowed because 64 is not a perfect cube
A polynomial can have two different complete factorizations, so both are right
responses.answer: a⁴ + 4a² + 16 is not prime: it is the product of the two quadratic factors from the squares-first method, so both methods agree

steps.title: Which pattern first?
steps.instruction: When a polynomial is both a difference of squares and a difference of cubes, factor the squares first; the cube patterns then finish the job. Cubes first leaves a fourth-degree factor that is harder to break apart.

steps.title: Adding zero
steps.instruction: A trinomial can sometimes be turned into a difference of squares by adding and subtracting the same term. Example: x⁴ + x² + 1 = (x⁴ + 2x² + 1) − x² = (x² + 1)² − x² = (x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1).

hints: a⁶ − 64 = (a³)² − 8², so the first step is (a³ − 8)(a³ + 8).
a⁴ + 8a² + 16 is a perfect square trinomial.
4a² is the square of which monomial?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. a⁶ is the square of…

solutionReview.headline: Squares first; then show the cubes-first quartic splits into the same quadratics.
reasoning: a⁴ + 4a² + 16 = (a² + 4)² − (2a)² = (a² + 2a + 4)(a² − 2a + 4), so the two methods give the same factors.
solutionReview.connection: A complete factorization is unique apart from the order of the factors and their signs, so two correct methods can never truly disagree.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at a⁴ + 4a² + 16 as if it were prime: adding and subtracting 4a² makes it a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. Jordan factored $8x^3 + 27$ as $(2x + 3)(4x^2 + 12x + 9)$. Test Jordan’s answer with a number, find the error, and fix it.

responses.label: What went wrong?
options: Jordan’s trinomial is (2x + 3)², but a sum of cubes needs a² − ab + b²
27 is not a perfect cube, so 8x³ + 27 is prime
Nothing: different values at x = 1 are allowed
responses.answer: Jordan’s trinomial is (2x + 3)², but a sum of cubes needs a² − ab + b²

hints: Substitute x = 1 into both expressions and compare.
Write 8x³ + 27 = (2x)³ + 3³, so a = 2x and b = 3.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If two expressions are equivalent, then at x = 1 they…

solutionReview.headline: One number can prove a factorization wrong; the pattern fixes it.
reasoning: At x = 1: 8 + 27 = 35, but (5)(25) = 125, so Jordan’s factorization is wrong.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) with a = 2x and b = 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Using (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² for the trinomial: the sum-of-cubes factor is a² − ab + b².
solutionReview.connection: A substitution test can prove a factorization wrong, never right: only multiplying back can prove it right.

questions.prompt: Structure and parameters. (a) Find every integer $k$ for which $x^2 + kx - 12$ factors over the integers. (b) Find every value of $b$ for which $4x^2 + bx + 9$ is a perfect square trinomial.

responses.label: (a) Every possible k, as a set
(b) Every possible b, as a set

hints: List the factor pairs of −12; k is the sum of each pair.
For 4x² + bx + 9 to be a perfect square, 4x² and 9 must be the squares of the two terms of a binomial.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If x² + kx − 12 = (x + m)(x + p), then k equals…

solutionReview.headline: Factor pairs give the sums; squares give the middle term.
reasoning: (a) The pairs with product −12 are 1 and −12, −1 and 12, 2 and −6, −2 and 6, 3 and −4, −3 and 4. Their sums are −11, 11, −4, 4, −1 and 1.
(b) 4x² = (2x)² and 9 = 3², so the trinomial is (2x + 3)² = 4x² + 12x + 9 or (2x − 3)² = 4x² − 12x + 9.
solutionReview.commonError: Listing only positive sums: a pair like 3 and −4 gives k = −1.

questions.prompt: Plan before you factor. Sort each polynomial by the FIRST step of factoring it completely.

categories.label: Difference of squares, or sum or difference of cubes

steps.title: A factoring plan
steps.instruction: 1. Take out a GCF. 2. Count the terms: two terms — squares or cubes; three terms — a trinomial method or quadratic form; four terms — grouping. 3. Check every factor again.

hints: Always check for a GCF before anything else.
Compare exponents: is one exponent twice another, such as x⁴ and x², or x⁶ and x³?
A sum of two squares, such as x² + 9, is prime.

solutionReview.headline: GCF first; then count the terms and compare the exponents.
reasoning: GCF first: 3x³ − 12x = 3x(x² − 4) = 3x(x − 2)(x + 2), and 4x² + 16 = 4(x² + 4), where x² + 4 is prime.
Quadratic form: x⁴ − 10x² + 9 = (x² − 1)(x² − 9) and x⁶ − 9x³ + 8 = (x³ − 1)(x³ − 8), because one exponent is twice the other.
Prime: x² + 9 is a sum of squares, and 2x² + 3x + 5 has no integer pair with product 10 and sum 3.
solutionReview.answerSummary: GCF: 3x³ − 12x, 4x² + 16. Quadratic form: x⁴ − 10x² + 9, x⁶ − 9x³ + 8. Squares or cubes: 49m² − 81n², 125 − 8y³. Grouping: the two four-term polynomials. Prime: x² + 9, 2x² + 3x + 5.
solutionReview.commonError: 4x² + 16 is not prime: its GCF, 4, comes out first, even though the x² + 4 that is left is prime.

questions.prompt: Modeling. An open box is made from a 12-inch by 8-inch sheet of cardboard by cutting a square with side $x$ inches from each corner and folding up the sides. Its volume is $V(x) = 4x^3 - 40x^2 + 96x$. Factor $V(x)$ completely, then connect the factors to the box.

responses.label: The base measures (12 − 2x) by (8 − 2x) and the height is x. How does that match your factorization?
options: It does not match, so the factorization is wrong
The base is x by x, and 4 is the height
(12 − 2x)(8 − 2x) = 96 − 4x², so the factors do not match

responses.label: Which values of x describe a real box?

hints: Every term contains 4x.
After the GCF, find two numbers with product 24 and sum −10.
Each side of the base must be positive: 8 − 2x > 0.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Cutting x inches from both ends of the 8-inch side leaves…

solutionReview.headline: Factor, then read the factors as the box.
reasoning: The box is x high with base (12 − 2x)(8 − 2x) = 2(6 − x) · 2(4 − x): the same factors, with two signs moved.
Every dimension must be positive: x > 0 and 8 − 2x > 0, so 0 < x < 4.
solutionReview.commonError: Answering x(12 − 2x)(8 − 2x): each binomial still has a common factor of 2.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: ${{k}}x^3 {{B|signed}}x^2 - {{Cabs}}x {{D|signed}}$
hints: Take out the GCF first.
Group the first two terms and the last two terms; the binomial left in each group should match.
Check the factors you have left: one is a difference of squares.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is the GCF of all four terms?

solutionReview.headline: GCF, grouping, then the difference of squares.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at {{k}}(x² − {{m2}})(x {{p|signed}}): x² − {{m2}} is still a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: $x^4 {{s|signed}}x^2 - {{P}}$
hints: Substitute u = x²: you need two numbers with product −{{P}} and sum {{s}}.
After substituting back, one factor is a difference of squares and the other is a sum, which is prime.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which substitution turns this polynomial into a quadratic?

solutionReview.headline: Quadratic form, then the difference of squares.
reasoning: x² − {{m2}} = (x − {{m}})(x + {{m}}), and x² + {{n}} is a sum of squares, which is prime.
solutionReview.commonError: Factoring x² + {{n}}: a sum of squares does not factor over the real numbers.

questions.prompt: Factor completely over the integers: $3x^4 + 5x^2 - 2$ and $x^8 - 1$.
hints: For the first, use u = x² and the ac method.
x⁸ = (x⁴)²: use the difference of squares more than once.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x⁸ is the square of…

solutionReview.headline: Quadratic form; then repeated differences of squares.
reasoning: 3u² + 5u − 2: a · c = −6, and 6 and −1 work: 3u² + 6u − u − 2 = 3u(u + 2) − (u + 2) = (3u − 1)(u + 2). Substituting back: (3x² − 1)(x² + 2), and neither factor factors over the integers.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at (x⁴ + 1)(x⁴ − 1): x⁴ − 1 is still a difference of squares, twice over.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: $(2x - 1)^2 - 5(2x - 1) + 6$. Substitute $u = 2x - 1$ first.
hints: Factor the trinomial in u.
Substitute back and simplify each factor. Does any factor still have a common factor?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If u = 2x − 1, then u − 3 equals…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, factor, substitute back — and look for a GCF.
solutionReview.commonError: (2x − 3)(2x − 4) is not completely factored: 2x − 4 has a common factor of 2.

questions.prompt: Challenge: a sum that factors. $x^4 + 64$ has no GCF and is a sum of squares, yet it factors over the integers. Add and subtract the right term to make a difference of squares, then factor completely.
hints: Expand (x² + 8)². What must be subtracted to get back to x⁴ + 64?
The term you subtract is a perfect square: write it as (something)².

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a + b)² expands to…

solutionReview.headline: Complete the square, then use the difference of squares.
reasoning: 16x² = (4x)², so this is a difference of squares: (x² + 8 − 4x)(x² + 8 + 4x).
Neither quadratic has real zeros (each discriminant is 16 − 32 < 0), so the factorization is complete.
solutionReview.commonError: Calling x⁴ + 64 prime because it is a sum of squares: a sum of FOURTH powers like this one can still factor into quadratics.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: ${{k}}x^4 {{sk3|signed}}x$
hints: Take out the GCF, including the x.
What is left is a sum or difference of two cubes: write the constant as a cube.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), the middle sign of the trinomial is…
options: the same as the binomial’s sign
the opposite of the binomial’s sign
scaffold.correct: the opposite of the binomial’s sign

solutionReview.headline: GCF, then the cube pattern.
solutionReview.commonError: Taking out only {{k}}: every term also contains x.

questions.prompt: Use three techniques. Factor completely: $2x^5 - 2x^3 - 54x^2 + 54$.
hints: Take out the GCF, then group the first two terms and the last two terms.
Both binomial factors still factor: one by squares, one by cubes.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x⁵ − x³ factors as…

solutionReview.headline: GCF, grouping, then squares and cubes.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping after grouping: x² − 1 and x³ − 27 both factor again.

questions.prompt: For all values of $x$, $x^3+{{p}}x^2+{{k}}x+t=(x+{{p}})(x^2+{{k}})$. What is the value of $t$?

optionRationales.{{t}}: Multiplying out, the constant term of (x + {{p}})(x² + {{k}}) is {{p}} · {{k}} = {{t}}.
optionRationales.{{dSum}}: {{dSum}} adds {{p}} and {{k}}; the constant term of a product comes from multiplying the constant terms.
optionRationales.{{dSquaredFirst}}: {{dSquaredFirst}} squares {{p}}; the constant term multiplies one constant from each factor.
optionRationales.{{dCollectedAll}}: {{dCollectedAll}} adds the coefficients {{p}} and {{k}} to the constant; t is only the constant term.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply out and compare constant terms.
reasoning: The constant terms must match, so t = {{p}} · {{k}} = {{t}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding {{p}} and {{k}}: the constant term of a product is the product of the constant terms.

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression and preserve equivalence.
supportHints: Use polynomial operations, factor structure, or polynomial division as appropriate.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The constant term of a product of two polynomials is…
options: the product of their constant terms
the sum of their constant terms
scaffold.correct: the product of their constant terms

questions.prompt: Group three and one. Factor $x^2 - 6x + 9 - 4y^2$ completely: the first three terms form a perfect square trinomial, which turns the whole expression into a difference of squares.
hints: x² − 6x + 9 is a perfect square trinomial.
4y² = (2y)². Use A² − B² = (A − B)(A + B).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A² − B² factors as…

solutionReview.headline: A perfect square minus a perfect square.
solutionReview.commonError: Grouping the last two terms: 9 − 4y² = (3 − 2y)(3 + 2y), which does not combine with x² − 6x.

questions.prompt: Parameters. (a) Find every positive integer $c$ for which $x^2 + 7x + c$ factors over the integers. (b) $x^3 + kx^2 + 4x + 12$ factors by grouping as $(x^2 + 4)(x + k)$. Find $k$.

responses.label: (a) Every positive c, as a set

hints: For (a), c is the product of two numbers whose sum is 7.
For (b), expand (x² + 4)(x + k) and compare constant terms.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If x² + 7x + c = (x + m)(x + n), then m + n equals…

solutionReview.headline: Sums and products of factor pairs; matching coefficients.
reasoning: (a) Positive pairs with sum 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, so c = 6, 10 or 12. Two negative numbers cannot add to 7.
(b) (x² + 4)(x + k) = x³ + kx² + 4x + 4k, so 4k = 12 and k = 3.
solutionReview.commonError: In (b), k is not 12: expanding (x² + 4)(x + k) gives the constant 4k, so 4k = 12.

questions.prompt: Modeling. A box has volume $V(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 12$ cubic feet, and each of its dimensions is a linear expression in $x$ with integer coefficients. Find the dimensions, then use them when $x = 5$.

responses.label: The height is the shortest dimension. Height when x = 5 (feet)
Which values of x describe a real box?

hints: Group the first two terms and the last two terms.
Every dimension must be positive; the shortest one decides.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For a box, every dimension must be…

solutionReview.headline: Factor by grouping, then read the dimensions.
reasoning: At x = 5 the dimensions are 8, 3 and 7 feet, so the height is 3 ft.
V(5) = 8 · 3 · 7 = 168 cubic feet, the same as substituting 5 into V(x).
x − 2 > 0 makes all three dimensions positive, so x > 2.
solutionReview.commonError: Choosing x > −3: every dimension, x − 2 included, must be positive.

questions.prompt: The polynomial $P(x)=x^3+{{b}}x^2+{{c}}x+k$ has factor $x+{{p}}$. If $k$ is positive, what is the value of $k$?

solutionReview.headline: A factor x + p means P(−p) = 0.
reasoning: If x + {{p}} is a factor, then P(x) = (x + {{p}}) · Q(x), so P(−{{p}}) = 0 · Q(−{{p}}) = 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Substituting x = {{p}}: the factor x + {{p}} is 0 at x = −{{p}}, not at x = {{p}}.

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression and preserve equivalence.
supportHints: Use polynomial operations, factor structure, or polynomial division as appropriate.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If x + p is a factor of P(x), which input makes P(x) equal 0?

questions.prompt: Factoring proves things. Factor $n^3 - n$ completely, then use the factors to explain why $n^3 - n$ is divisible by 6 for every integer $n$.

responses.label: Why is n³ − n divisible by 6 for every integer n?
options: n − 1, n and n + 1 are three consecutive integers: one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even
n³ − n is always even, and every even number is divisible by 6
6 divides n³ for every integer n
n − 1 and n + 1 are always both even
responses.answer: n − 1, n and n + 1 are three consecutive integers: one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even

hints: Take out the GCF n, then factor the difference of squares.
Write the three factors in order from least to greatest.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Among any three consecutive integers, how many are multiples of 3?

solutionReview.headline: Factor, then read the factors.
reasoning: These are three consecutive integers: one of them is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even, so the product is a multiple of 2 · 3 = 6.
solutionReview.answerSummary: n(n − 1)(n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers; 120
solutionReview.commonError: Showing only that n³ − n is even: divisibility by 6 needs a factor of 2 and a factor of 3.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: $(x {{a|signed}})^2 - {{b2}}$
hints: {{b2}} = {{b}}², so this is a difference of squares A² − B² where A is the whole binomial.
Simplify each factor by combining the constants.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A² − B² factors as…

solutionReview.headline: Treat the binomial as one quantity.
solutionReview.commonError: Expanding first works but takes longer: x² {{ta|xterm}} {{cc|signed}} must then be factored back.

questions.prompt: Factor completely: $x^4 - {{s}}x^2 + {{P}}$

solutionReview.headline: Quadratic form, then two differences of squares.
